### Prerequisites

In this text, we will present a new representation of the abacuses studied so far: the Soroban and the Suanpan (算盤). Therefore, we recommend reading the previous text (<htcite0>), for a better understanding of this text.

source.page: Grandes ordens com o Soroban e Suanpan (算盤)

text.text:
### Introduction

In the West, we currently use numbers whose values increase from right to left: the units are on the right and, as new digits are added, the values of the orders increase (<htcite0>).

But, as we have also seen, the indigenous peoples of *Abya Yala* (America) represent their numbers vertically, with the smaller numbers at the bottom and the larger numbers at the top (<htcite1>).

When studying the abacuses so far, we have always represented numbers from right to left, as we generally do with our numbers. Based on what we have learned about the indigenous peoples of *Abya Yala*, let us reflect:

Reflection 1: Both there and here

Could we represent numbers on the abacus, vertically, Schyoty (счёты), in the same way that the indigenous peoples of Abya Yala (America) represent their numbers?

### History

When studying the Soroban (算盤), we learned that it is a tool built in Japan (Nippon-koku or Nihon-koku, 日本国) (<htcite0>). However, as we saw next, it originated from another abacus, the Suanpan (算盤), developed in China (<htcite1>).

The relationship between the two is explicit by the way numbers are represented, in addition to the same characters used in writing. Regarding the Schyoty (счёты) abacus, presented in **Figure 1**, this relationship is not as evident
Figure 1: Example of an abacus used in Russia. © Trustees of the British Museum ().

#### Possible origins

When studying the mathematical tools used in Russia, Alexei Volkov raises important points about how this instrument could have arrived in the country.

Although there are citations indicating that the instrument was already present in Russia around <htdate0>, it is not possible to state that its origin is China (Zhōngguó, 中國) (<htcite0>).

Besides, in his work, Alexei Volkov also mentions that research such as Simonov's proposes that the abacus used in Russia could be even older, possibly dating back to the 13th century, according to the Gregorian calendar. However, this hypothesis seems unlikely (<htcite1>).

Despite the difficulties of dating and even defining its origin, the Russian abacus brings some interesting features, which we will begin to study.

### The Schyoty (счёты)

When looking at the Schyoty (счёты) in **Figure 1**, we can observe that it is represented vertically. However, as Jessica Amarteifio shows in her work, it is also possible to use it horizontally (<htcite0>).

Another point we should highlight when comparing the (счёты) with the previous abacuses is the fact that there is no bar in it where, when moving a marker closer, it comes to represent a certain value. Nor are there markers with value 5. All markers have the same value 1. As a consequence of these differences, to represent a value on the abacus, we must position all markers on one side of the rod and represent a number by moving the necessary markers to the opposite side (<htcite1>).

### Representing on the Schyoty (счёты)

In *History Tracers*, we will not use the abacus as presented by Jessica Amarteifio. Nevertheless, we would like to share her teaching method, informing that when all markers are positioned at the top, the abacus will represent the number zero. As we move the markers downward toward the bottom, we will begin to represent other numbers (<htcite0>).

Similarly, when the abacus is in a vertical position and all markers are on the right side, we will be representing the number zero. As we move the markers to the left, we will represent other numbers.

To make this clearer, do the following exercise by representing the requested number. By clicking **Restart**, a new number will be displayed, and you can practice again.
